The Effect of Gait Stability Based on Two Types of Impact Strategies for Two-Link Walking and Brachiating Robots

Alan Estrada Flores1    Nelson Rosa Jr.1
††tocauthor: Alan Estrada Flores and Nelson Rosa Jr.††institute: Illinois Institute of Technology, Chicago IL 60616, USA

1 Introduction

The two-link walking models of Garcia et al. (1998) and Goswami et al. (1998) and the brachiating model of Gomes and Ruina (2005) have provided valuable insight into the mechanics of limbed locomotion in the fields of biomechanics and robotics. Figure 1 shows example motions of the model in Gomes and Ruina (2005). In addition to contributions to human and robot gait analysis, these works show that the underlying impulsive dynamics exhibit rich nonlinear phenomena.

For bipedal walking, these results include the existence of passive dynamic walking gaits (i.e., unactuated periodic walking motions of the impulsive dynamics), period-doubling bifurcations, strange attractors, and chaotic motion Garcia et al. (1998); Goswami et al. (1998). A large body of work has since explored variations of these canonical walking models with the addition of, e.g., springs and dampers, limbs, and forcing functions (see Safartoobi et al. (2022) and references therein). Common results include the existence of period-doubling (PD) bifurcations and their associated route to chaos. The results for brachiation are much more sparse, but a core result is the existence of unstable passive dynamic gaits with zero energy loss across impacts and energetically-conservative swing dynamics Gomes and Ruina (2005). These results have been extended to show the existence of stable and unstable passive dynamic and actuated gaits and observations of fold (FD) and Neimark-Sacker (NS) bifurcations Rosa et al. (2012); Rosa and Lynch (2013).

Given past work, a gap that still persists is the lack of a unified bifurcation analysis of two-link models and their set of walking and brachiating gaits Rosa and Lynch (2013). Ultimately, both of these fields study the same equations of motion, but results are only reported in isolation. Specifically, both fields analyze the behavior of fixed points of a discrete step-to-step map. The map represents the continuous swing motion of the robot as it pivots about its hand or foot followed by an instantaneous plastic collision with an inclined surface. Because of the bilateral symmetry of many two-link models, a periodic motion (i.e., a gait) can be identified after just one step and a relabeling of coordinates Garcia et al. (1998); Goswami et al. (1998); Safartoobi et al. (2022); Rosa et al. (2012); Rosa and Lynch (2013). The periodicity of a fixed point is thus defined with respect to the number of steps the robot takes. In other words, a gait that takes nn steps is a period-nn fixed point.

Another understudied facet in both fields is the switching function of the impulsive dynamics. In our numerical study, we explore a step-to-step map under state-based switching (SBS) and time-based switching (TBS) strategies. In SBS, a collision occurs whenever the distance between the surface and the end effector of the robot (serving as a foot for walking or hand for brachiating) is zero. In the literature, SBS is the de facto choice with the slope of the surface treated as a free parameter of the system. For TBS, collisions occur after a pre-determined duration of time has elapsed. In this case, switching time is the free parameter. TBS is a viable control option for robots in vertical environments (e.g., Rosa et al. (2012); Mbewe and Boje (2025)) as contacts can be made at any point in time on the surface.

As further motivation for this study, an interesting aspect of switching strategies is that both strategies produce the same set of period-one gaits. We omit a formal proof as this is intuitively true. For every gait under SBS, we can take a stopwatch to determine the switching time, and, for every gait under TBS, we can record the slope at the switching time. Given this fact, we still observe different long-term gait behaviors across impacts depending on the switching strategy. This leads to our core contributions.

1.1 Statement of Contributions

In this paper, we explore the impulsive dynamics common to single-joint, two-link models of walking and brachiating gaits with respect to slope and switching time. In particular, we expand on the observations made in Rosa and Lynch (2013) with respect to how the stability of a gait and bifurcations encountered within a family of gaits change under TBS and SBS of the impulsive dynamics. Our contributions are

  1. 1.

    A numerical study of gait stability under two switching strategies. We study the stability of gait families with respect to time-based and state-based switching functions of the impulsive dynamics. When there is a loss of stability in a gait family, we observe PD, NS, and FD bifurcations.

  2. 2.

    An exploration of the role of symmetry with gait families. Two-link models with bilateral symmetry have period-one gait families that are mirror images of each other about the switching time axis. We investigate the evolution of unstable gaits in these families for one such model. In particular, we find that near FD bifurcations, unstable gaits that start in one gait family converge to stable gaits in the mirrored family of gaits under TBS.

Figure 2 provides a visual summary of these contributions.

2 The Two-Link Model

The parameters mim_{i} and IiI_{i} are the masses and moments of inertia about the center of mass of each link, respectively. The pivot point (qx,qy)(q_{x},q_{y}) is fixed throughout the swing motion. At impact, the post-impact values are fully determined by the pre-impact values of q1q_{1} and q2q_{2}. For convenience, we use a reduced configuration vector q=[q1,q2]T∈ℝ2q=[q_{1},q_{2}]^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{2} with state vector x=[qT,q˙T]T∈ℝ4x=[q^{T},\dot{q}^{T}]^{T}\in\mathbb{R}^{4}.

2.1 The Continuous Dynamics

The continuous dynamics of the model during the swing phase are those of a double pendulum. The equations can be written in standard form for mechanical systems and solved for q¨\ddot{q} such that

M⁡(q⁡(t))​q¨​(t)+C⁡(q⁡(t),q˙​(t))​q˙​(t)+g⁡(q⁡(t))=0,M(q(t))\ddot{q}(t)+C(q(t),\dot{q}(t))\dot{q}(t)+g(q(t))=0,

where A=[110−1]A=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}1&1\\ 0&-1\end{smallmatrix}\right] and b=[π0]b=\left[\begin{smallmatrix}\pi\\ 0\end{smallmatrix}\right] achieves a relabeling of the coordinate system; Δ⁡(x)∈ℝ2\Delta(x)\in\mathbb{R}^{2} is our impact map relating the pre-impact velocity q˙−\dot{q}^{-} to the post-impact velocity q˙+\dot{q}^{+} such that q˙+=Δ⁡(q−)​q˙−\dot{q}^{+}=\Delta(q^{-})\dot{q}^{-}; and a1=2​β​δ​κ1−2​κ1​κ2a_{1}=2\beta\delta\kappa_{1}-2\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}, a2=δ2−2​κ1​κ2+δ2​cos⁡(2​q2)a_{2}=\delta^{2}-2\kappa_{1}\kappa_{2}+\delta^{2}\cos(2q_{2}), and a3=(β​κ1−κ2+(β−1)​δ​c2)a_{3}=(\beta\kappa_{1}-\kappa_{2}+(\beta-1)\delta c_{2}).

2.3 The Switching Function

We define the switching function ϕ\phi as

ϕ⁡(x⁡(t,x0),t)={sin⁡(σ⁡(x0)−σ⁡(x⁡(t,x0)))for SBSt−τfor TBS,\phi(x(t,x_{0}),t)=\begin{cases}\sin(\sigma(x_{0})-\sigma(x(t,x_{0})))&\text{for SBS}\\ t-\tau&\text{for TBS},\end{cases} (3)

where σ⁡(x⁡(t))=π−q2​(t)2−q1​(t)\sigma(x(t))=\frac{\pi-q_{2}(t)}{2}-q_{1}(t) is the instantaneous slope at time tt. We expand on our definition of σ\sigma in the sequel. The sin\sin term is more straightforward to explain: slopes that differ in multiples of π\pi represent the same inclined surface (e.g., level ground locomotion can be represented with σ\sigma values of k​πk\pi, k∈ℤk\in\mathbb{Z}).

2.3.1 Defining the Walking Surface

As is common in the literature, a pre-defined value of σ\sigma determines the surface incline. In our work, we introduce the notion of an instantaneous slope σ⁡(x)=π−q22−q1\sigma(x)=\frac{\pi-q_{2}}{2}-q_{1}. This equation for σ\sigma measures the angle between the straight line connecting the feet (or hands) of the robot and the horizontal. The quantity always coincides with the value of any pre-defined surface incline at the beginning and end of a step; e.g., for a post-impact state x0x_{0}, any pre-defined slope must equal σ⁡(x0)\sigma(x_{0}).

Remark 1

Typically, q1q_{1} and q2q_{2} are chosen so that the robot is on a pre-defined slope σ\sigma. Here, we simply do the converse. Relative to other works, we eliminate σ\sigma as an unnecessary free parameter, especially when computing gait families with numerical continuation. In the end, there is no loss of generality. For any work that treats σ\sigma as a free parameter, a little bit of geometry will show that the value of σ\sigma can be determined by the configuration of the paper’s two-link model.

3 Methodology and Results

The physical parameters of our study are chosen to match those of Gomes and Ruina (2005). The approximate values are β=18.13\beta=18.13, δ1=0.50\delta_{1}=0.50, δ2=0.50\delta_{2}=0.50, γ=1\gamma=1, κ1=0.28\kappa_{1}=0.28, and κ2=8.84\kappa_{2}=8.84. We compute the initial gaits of each gait family using the methods outlined in Gomes and Ruina (2005) for brachiating and Rosa and Lynch (2014) for walking. We then use a pseudo-arclength continuation method with a fixed step size of 0.001. The algorithm runs until it either fails or generates 50,000 points. For period-one fixed points, stability is determined by assessing the magnitude of the eigenvalues of the linearized impulsive dynamics. To study the long-term evolution of unstable gaits with respect to switching strategy, we simulate a gait across 1,000 impacts and then analyze the impact sequence. The code used to generate these solutions and visualize the bifurcations is available at https://github.com/aestr6/TWOLINK_NODYCON.

3.1 The Big Picture

Figure 3 provides a global view of passive dynamic families of walking and brachiating gaits as curves projected onto a switching-time-joint-angle plane. To distinguish between TBS and SBS, we use τ\tau to denote an independent switching time parameter and τ⁡(x0)\tau(x_{0}) as a state-dependent switching time, respectively.

Overall, there are four types of qualitatively similar motions that can be found within each gait family. Each motion corresponds to walking or brachiating above or below a surface (e.g., the example gaits of Figure 1). A more nuanced exploration of gait families with respect to these motions can be found in Rosa and Lynch (2013). With respect to switching strategies, the plots highlight differences in gait stability and bifurcations. For example, three of the curves have regions of stable gaits under an SBS strategy and contain the three simple bifurcation types. In contrast, TBS only has two gait families with stable regions. These regions are smaller and undergo either NS or FD bifurcations once the gaits are no longer stable. In the remaining sections, we further explore the top-most curve and the bottom right-most curve in these plots.

3.2 Exploring a Brachiating Family of Gaits

The top-most curve in Figure 3 is a curve of brachiating gaits with gaits along the curve that will qualitatively look like the motions in the bottom row of Figure 1. Figure 4 compares the evolution of gaits on the curve under SBS as slope is varied and under TBS as switching time is varied. For slopes ranging from −2.0∘-2.0^{\circ} to −24.5∘-24.5^{\circ}, under SBS, the period-one fixed points are stable, resulting in gaits that remain on the initial gait family. At σcrit≈−24.57∘\sigma_{\text{crit}}\approx-24.57^{\circ}, the stable period-one gait loses stability through a PD bifurcation, giving rise to a stable period-two gait. This transition is confirmed by an eigenvalue crossing the unit circle at −1-1. Note that SBS always has a marginally stable eigenvalue at +1+1, as expected for hybrid systems with state-defined switching surfaces Bainov and Simeonov (1993).

The same brachiating family exhibits different stability properties under TBS. From τ=1.90\tau=1.90 to 2.442.44, the period-one fixed points are stable along the brachiating branch. At τcrit≈2.14\tau_{\text{crit}}\approx 2.14, an NS bifurcation occurs. The bifurcation is confirmed by the complex conjugate eigenvalues crossing the unit circle, with values λ1,2≈−0.88±0.47​i\lambda_{1,2}\approx-0.88\pm 0.47i. Beyond the NS bifurcation, trajectories converge onto closed invariant curves. The bottom-right plot in Figure 4 shows 1,000 successive impacts spiraling away from the unstable fixed point toward a stable closed invariant curve.

3.3 Fold Bifurcations and Symmetry in Time-Based Switching

The NS bifurcation is only one boundary of the stable region shown in Figure 4. The opposite end exhibits an FD bifurcation, shown in Figure 5. This bifurcation occurs at τcrit≈1.92\tau_{\text{crit}}\approx 1.92 and is characterized by the crossing of the unit circle by an eigenvalue at +1. Figure 5 depicts the evolution of post-impact states following this bifurcation.

Due to the bilateral symmetry of the system, if (x0,τ,σ)(x_{0},\tau,\sigma) is a gait, then so is (−x0,τ,−σ)(-x_{0},\tau,-\sigma). The resulting motion is identical, but simply reflected (e.g., a gait that walks to the left instead walks to the right). Consequently, every gait family naturally possesses a mirrored counterpart. This can be seen in Figure 5, which shows a segment of a brachiating curve and its mirrored segment below the q1=0q_{1}=0 axis. Notably, trajectories originating near the unstable regions of one family are shown to converge into either the stable domain of their original or mirrored gait families along directions of constant τ\tau. For instance, at label A (τ=1.93\tau=1.93) and D (τ=2.13\tau=2.13), the gaits converge onto the stable region of the primary curve. Alternatively, at B (τ=1.97\tau=1.97) and C (τ=2.02\tau=2.02), the gaits converge onto the stable region of the mirrored curve. This behavior highlights the complex basins of attraction that arise from the system’s geometric symmetries.

Beyond the stable region, no stable period-one solutions remain. Consequently, the trajectories converge to closed invariant curves near the NS bifurcation point.

3.4 Exploring a Walking Family of Gaits After a Fall

Given Figure 3, we see that stable walking gaits only exist for SBS. While walking gaits under SBS are the most explored in the literature, we present results on an unexplored avenue of research. If we continue applying the SBS policy, where do unstable walking gaits (UWGs) go if the robot is in environments that allow it to transition between locomoting above and below a surface (e.g., power lines Mbewe and Boje (2025))?

Figure 6 addresses this question for the parameters of our model. The plot shows the gait families under SBS from Figure 3 projected onto a slope-switching-time plane. Instead of terminating the simulation after the robot falls, we continue to impact the surface and plot the results after 1,000 impacts. The final impacts are shown in cyan. UWGs near the stable walking region (σ∈[3.29∘,3.86∘]\sigma\in[3.29^{\circ},3.86^{\circ}]) settle into a PD periodic orbit. After the PD structure breaks down, the UWGs generally converge to stable period-one brachiating gaits (σ∈[4.06∘,24.47∘]\sigma\in[4.06^{\circ},24.47^{\circ}]). When the region of stable period-one brachiating gaits ends, the UWGs then converge to the PD orbits of brachiating gaits after crossing the PD bifurcation point on the brachiating curve at σ≈24.57∘\sigma\approx 24.57^{\circ}.

While most UWGs converge to the period-one brachiating gait family below the UWG branch, there are UWGs that converge to brachiating motions above the unstable curve near τ≈2.7\tau\approx 2.7. The inset plot in the middle provides a snapshot of five of these gaits. The stable gaits are either period-one or period-two fixed points in the region.

4 Conclusion

The comparative analysis of SBS and TBS strategies reveals fundamental differences in the stability of passive dynamic walking and brachiating gaits. Most notably, we demonstrate that SBS induces FD, PD, and NS bifurcations, whereas TBS results in NS and FD bifurcations. Additional results include the discovery of intertwined basins of attraction for mirrored sets of gaits for models with bilateral symmetry under TBS. Furthermore, we identify basins of attraction that exist for unstable period-one walking gaits under SBS after the robot falls, which converge to stable brachiating gaits.

To the best of our knowledge, this is the first combined analysis showing the connection between walking and brachiating gaits in the space of passive dynamic walking gaits. However, we stopped short of investigating the chaotic regimes present with our model. Future work will be dedicated to formally analyzing routes to chaos and identifying potential strange attractors in the gait space.
